ABSTRACT


Population

aging

has

been

accompanied

by

an

increasing

prevalence

of

chronic

diseases,

higher

hospitalization

rates,

and

poorer

clinical

outcomes

among

older

adults,

highlighting

the

need

to

identify

factors

associated

with

long-term

mortality

in

this

population.

The

aim

of

this

dissertation

was

to

identify

clinical

and

nutritional

factors

associated

with

mortality

up

to

ten

years

after

hospital

discharge

among

older

adults

with

and

without

type

2

diabetes

mellitus

(T2DM).

This

study

consisted

of

a

retrospective

reanalysis

of

an

originally

prospective

cohort

conducted

at

the

Hospital

de

Clínicas

de

Porto

Alegre

(HCPA),

Brazil,

between

July

2015

and

December

2016,

including

patients

aged

60

years

or

older

admitted

to

medical

wards.

Follow-up

was

extended

to

up

to

ten

years

after

hospital

discharge

through

electronic

medical

records,

telephone

interviews

with

patients

or

their

relatives,

and

consultation

of

the

Mortality

Information

System

of

the

Rio

Grande

do

Sul

State

Health

Department.

Sociodemographic

characteristics,

comorbidities,

nutritional

status

assessed

by

the

Mini

Nutritional

Assessment

(MNA),

sarcopenia

according

to

the

European

Working

Group

on

Sarcopenia

in

Older

People

2

(EWGSOP2)

criteria,

in-hospital

weight

loss,

and

serum

albumin

levels

were

evaluated.

The

primary

outcome

was

all-cause

mortality,

and

data

were

analyzed

using

Kaplan–Meier

survival

curves

and

Cox

proportional

hazards

regression

models.

The

final

sample

comprised

588

participants,

with

a

mean

age

of

73.35

±

6.5

years;

51%

were

women

and

50.3%

had

T2DM.

During

the

ten-year

follow-up,

391

deaths

(66.5%)

were

recorded.

The

main

independent

predictors

of

mortality

were

older

age,

malnutrition

according

to

the

MNA,

in-hospital

weight

loss

and

sarcopenia,

and

lower

serum

albumin

levels,

whereas

T2DM

alone

was

not

independently

associated

with

long-term

mortality.

These

findings

demonstrate

that

markers

of

nutritional

status

and

muscle

health

have

greater

prognostic

value

for

long-term

mortality

than

the

isolated

presence

of

T2DM,

reinforcing

the

importance

of

systematically

assessing

sarcopenia

and

malnutrition

during

hospitalization

to

identify

older

adults

at

higher

risk

and

support

targeted

clinical

interventions.
